parsed.explanation: The division is genuinely protective: gender-identity anti-discrimination since 2008 (expanded 2025), facilities access protected (2013 ruling, 2023 law), hate-crime coverage since 2001 with a murder conviction, conversion-therapy ban, shield care law, and courts that actively rule for trans people (May 2026 hospital order, prison consent decree). But the combined regime adds a restrictive national layer the division cannot override: passport/visa marker bans, an entry cable directing refusal where documents or other evidence cast doubt on sex with possible lifetime fraud ineligibility, federally funded single-sex facility exclusion, documented immigration-detention abuse of trans people, and federal corrections conversion policies applying to anyone in federal custody. Visitor exposure runs chiefly through border screening and federal custody; local life is comparatively safe. Net: Reduced Risk, held below the pure-protection tier by the inescapable federal exposures.

entry_documents.exposure: Federal order ends X markers and requires M/F per assigned sex; Feb 2025 cable tells officers to refuse where document/record discrepancy or other evidence casts doubt on sex, and to consider lifetime fraud ineligibility for wilful misrepresentation. Trans travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, stranded abroad; eight foreign governments issued advisories.
entry_documents.protection: Division issues X/Intersex markers on birth certificates and X on IDs (resident-facing climate signal only); legal-aid FAQ guides trans travelers on documentation; existing X passports valid to expiry.
entry_documents.interaction: A visitor's documents are federally issued; the division's marker rules cannot cure a passport mismatch, and refusal would occur at the national border desk, not under division law.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal immigration custody: trans men report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; detentions of neighbouring-country citizens over visa issues documented. National corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style policies (haircut, hormone removal) from 2026 and stopped counting trans prisoners.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Division 2024 consent decree (specialized housing, $2.1m to ~400 inmates), 2019 settlement, hate-crime law. These bind division corrections, not federal immigration custody a visitor would enter.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Entry refusal or visa dispute moves a visitor into the federal system, where neither the division consent decree nor its anti-discrimination statute operates.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Federal order bars trans people from federally funded/owned single-sex facilities; national map shows 9+1 units with all-government-building bans and 4 states criminalising in certain circumstances (this division is not among them).
federal_state_facilities.protection: Division: 2013 civil-rights ruling, 2023 full bathroom-access law, public-accommodations anti-discrimination covering gender identity/expression since 2008, expanded 2025.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal funding conditions demonstrably override division protections (youth-care insurance suspension Oct 2026 shows the pattern); federally owned buildings in the division follow the federal rule.

care_services.exposure: A children's hospital suspended youth gender care under national pressure before being ordered to resume (compliance unresolved); federal rule blocks funds, forcing division public-insurance suspension from 13 Oct 2026 for residents.
care_services.protection: Division 2023 shield-and-safe-passage law, insurance mandates covering transition care since 2023, May 2026 high-court 5-2 order requiring care to resume, conversion-therapy ban re-strengthened May 2026. Private-pay visitor access documented as protected.
care_services.interaction: National funding and enforcement pressure reached into division hospitals despite division law — protection is real but demonstrably permeable at the federal layer.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National framing: EO terms 'chemical and surgical mutilation,' 'radical gender ideology' in enforcement guidance, May 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritising groups 'radically pro-transgender,' criminal-referral directive on schools; 66% public support for assigned-sex document rules.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division: hate-crime law covering gender identity since 2001 with penalty enhancements, 2009 first-degree-murder hate-crime conviction, gay-panic defence abolished 2020, comprehensive anti-discrimination enforcement.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Division law enforcement and courts operate protectively, but federal agencies setting tone and funding do not; street friction is locally cushioned, federal encounters are not.

minors_guardians.exposure: Three Nov 2026 ballot measures (sports ban, child surgery ban) pending; district-level sports bans adopted 2025; federal EO threatens criminal prosecution for facilitating a trans minor's social transition; federal care-funding cut from Oct 2026.
minors_guardians.protection: Division anti-bullying law covering gender identity, 2025 act requiring chosen names/pronouns and any uniform option, shield care law, court order restoring youth care, parental-consent minor marker changes.
minors_guardians.interaction: A visiting family's care needs are met privately under division law, but a school-age or care-seeking minor passes through federal funding and enforcement rules the division cannot disapply.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific figure for killings or violence against trans people, and no comparison to the general homicide rate appears in the sources. National bias statistics are sexual-orientation, not trans-specific, and undated for current prevalence.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Division hate-crime conviction with penalty enhancements (2009), bias-motivated-crime coverage since 2001, functioning courts.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Absence of a division violence figure in an otherwise rich dossier is mild positive signal only — this is not a thin-data jurisdiction, but the axis remains unquantified.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Unresolved: Nov 2026 ballot outcomes, compliance with the May 2026 care order, operation of document-change provisions after 1 Oct 2026, several federal orders partly enjoined or in litigation — practical exposure varies with which federal measures are operative at travel time.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Functioning courts ruling for trans people (5-2 and 8-1 2026 decisions), ACLU litigation against the passport policy, legal-aid FAQ, consent-decree remedies with payouts.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Remedies work FOR trans people inside the division but cannot reach border adjudication or federal custody, where the visitor's most severe documented exposures sit.

anchor_checks.comparison: Higher than 0.35-A: Vellandra's Visitor Conduct Register routinely bars trans visitors with no remedy. Here the entry exposure is narrower (discrepancy-triggered refusal plus fraud consideration, never automatic), division life carries full anti-discrimination and facilities protection, and active federal litigation exists. The border layer alone would not reach 0.35, but it keeps this well below the pure-protection tier.

Comparable in kind to 0.55-B's discretionary secondary screening, extended questioning and slow-to-reverse refusals — the national entry cable produces similar border friction with opaque criteria. Higher overall because inside the division the traveller encounters documented protections, functioning courts and low street exposure rather than only an administrative appeal desk.

Similar to 0.65-E: an immigration officer applying outdated/overreaching sex-disclosure practice, delays, an advocate FAQ, unresolved audit-level uncertainty. Lower than 0.65-E because detention is NOT barred by policy here — documented immigration-custody abuse of trans people, possible lifetime ineligibility, and federal conversion-style custody policy make the downside materially worse.

Below 0.75-C: Meridia's border recognises trans markers, trains officers, and offers compensation for unlawful holding. Here markers are federally restricted, refusal is instructed on sex doubt, lifetime fraud findings are conceivable, and documented federal custody abuse has no counterpart in 0.75-C. Division-level protections roughly match 0.75-C's tribunal quality, but the entry and custody layers drag the combined regime down.

parsed.synthesis: The operative system is a protective division nested inside a hostile and actively changing federal regime, and the two do not average — they stack at the stages a visitor cannot avoid. The border is the sharpest exposure: markers are federally restricted, officers are instructed to refuse on sex doubt, and a lifetime fraud finding is contemplated, with documented stranding of trans travelers and foreign-government advisories. Federal custody — the destination if entry fails — carries documented abuse and conversion-style policy the division's consent decree cannot reach. Inside the division, everyday life is unusually safe: protected facilities, comprehensive anti-discrimination, hate-crime law with a murder conviction, shield care law, and courts that rule for trans people. Federal funding pressure has already bent division services (youth-care insurance suspension; a hospital previously suspending care), proving the protection is permeable. Pending ballot measures add open uncertainty, not documented exposure. Adult-alone and adult-with-minor outcomes are similar; minors face pending sports/surgery ballot measures and federal care-funding cuts rather than custody risk.
